subject: science
objective: Read valence electrons for main-group elements from the periodic table; predict and explain the relative atomic radius, first ionization energy, and electronegativity of two elements from their positions; model ionic bonding as electron transfer to full shells and write binary ionic formulas from ion charges; model covalent bonding as shared pairs and complete simple Lewis structures; and classify a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic from electronegativity difference and element type.
prerequisites: Atoms have protons and neutrons in a nucleus with electrons around it
Atomic number is the number of protons; a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons
sources: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e, Section 6.5: Periodic Variations in Element Properties (https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/6-5-periodic-variations-in-element-properties)

OpenStax, Chemistry 2e, Sections 7.1 Ionic Bonding, 7.2 Covalent Bonding (electronegativity-difference guide and exceptions), and 7.3 Lewis Symbols and Structures (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e)

Chemistry LibreTexts, Reference Table A2: Electronegativity Values, Pauling scale (https://chem.libretexts.org/Ancillary_Materials/Reference/Reference_Tables/Atomic_and_Molecular_Properties/A2%3A_Electronegativity_Values)

Chemistry LibreTexts, Reference Table A3: Covalent Radii, single-bond values from Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832-2838 (https://chem.libretexts.org/Ancillary_Materials/Reference/Reference_Tables/Atomic_and_Molecular_Properties/A3%3A_Covalent_Radii)

Chemistry LibreTexts, Reference Table A6: Atomic Ionization Energies (https://chem.libretexts.org/Ancillary_Materials/Reference/Reference_Tables/Atomic_and_Molecular_Properties/A6%3A_Atomic_Ionization_Energies)
misconceptions: Atoms get bigger across a period because they have more electrons
Valence electrons equal the period number, or the group number for groups 13 to 18
Metals gain electrons and nonmetals lose them
Ionic formulas are 1:1, or have their subscripts swapped
Ionic compounds are made of separate molecules
Bonds are either fully ionic or fully covalent, with nothing in between
The shell model shows electrons orbiting in circles
modelLimitations: Shell (Bohr) diagrams are a counting model; the lesson says electrons do not travel in circular orbits.
Valence-electron counting, ion predictions, and data cover only the main-group elements of periods 1 to 5; other elements show name, number, and position with a note.
Atomic radius is the single-bond covalent radius (Cordero et al. 2008); noble gases are left blank because their values are not comparable.

Ga3+ and In3+ are described as keeping a filled shell of 18 rather than a noble-gas arrangement; tin's ions are flagged as an exception to the octet shortcut; hydrogen is described as usually sharing.
The ionic builder shows electrons moving one at a time as bookkeeping, and the lesson notes that ionic solids are lattices, not molecules.
The Lewis builder handles only neutral molecules with no formal charges and full octets (duet for H); it notes octet exceptions (BF3, SF6) and that O2 is paramagnetic in reality.
Molecules are drawn flat with approximate shapes; captions give the real geometry and bond angles.
Bond type uses the textbook guide (under 0.4 nonpolar, 0.4 to 1.8 polar covalent, over 1.8 ionic) alongside the metal/nonmetal rule, and says both are rules of thumb on a continuous scale.
Metallic bonding is mentioned only when two metals are picked.

Practice questions are generated from templates; trend comparisons use only pairs in the same row or column where the data follow the trend by a clear margin, and bond-type questions use only pairs where both rules of thumb agree.
